analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier to block big mergers and fine dominant companies that squeeze out competitors.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee on February 4, 2021 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite federal antitrust law so regulators can stop mergers that carry a real risk of reducing competition, including mergers that push down wages paid to workers. Very large mergers or deals that sharply concentrate a market would have to prove they don't harm competition, rather than the government having to prove harm. It would also let the government fine companies up to 15% of their US revenue for breaking antitrust laws, protect and reward whistleblowers who report price-fixing, and roughly triple the budgets of the two federal antitrust agencies.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers and workers, small businesses trying to compete against dominant firms, and suppliers forced to accept below-market prices by dominant buyers.

how_it_helps.text: Lowers the legal bar for blocking mergers from ones that 'substantially' lessen competition to ones that create an 'appreciable risk' of materially lessening it, and explicitly covers mergers that create monopsony power—the ability of a dominant buyer or employer to push down prices paid to suppliers or wages paid to workers.

Shifts the burden of proof to the merging companies for very large deals (over $5 billion) or deals that sharply increase market concentration, so the companies must show the deal won't harm competition instead of the government proving it will.

Makes it unlawful for dominant firms to engage in exclusionary conduct that risks harming competition, with civil penalties of up to 15% of a company's total US revenue, and adds civil penalties for Sherman Act violations.
Protects workers and contractors from retaliation for reporting antitrust violations and creates monetary rewards of up to 30% of criminal fines for whistleblowers whose tips lead to prosecutions.
Authorizes $484.5 million for the Justice Department's Antitrust Division and $651 million for the FTC for fiscal year 2022, funding the bill notes has fallen behind the growth of the economy.
Directs the Government Accountability Office to study how mergers and acquisitions have affected wages, employment, innovation, and new business formation.

Gives private plaintiffs who win antitrust damages the right to interest on their award from the date they filed, increasing compensation for businesses and consumers injured by anticompetitive conduct.

analysis.who_pays: Dominant corporations in concentrated markets—especially large technology platforms and other firms that acquire rivals, use exclusionary tactics, or fix prices—would face blocked mergers, litigation, and penalties up to 15% of US revenue. Companies planning large mergers would bear the cost of proving their deals are lawful.
analysis.who_pays_short: Dominant corporations and large merging firms

drawbacks.text: The 'appreciable risk' merger standard plus the shifted burden of proof for large deals could block or deter mergers that would have been pro-competitive or that generate real efficiencies, since companies bear the legal risk of proving a negative.

Civil penalties of up to 15% of total US revenue, and 30% of revenue in the affected line of commerce, are large enough that some firms might avoid aggressive but legal competitive conduct to steer clear of litigation risk.

The presumption of illegality for exclusionary conduct by firms with more than 50% market share relies on market-share measures that can misidentify genuinely dominant firms in fast-moving markets, inviting contested litigation over market definition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core purpose—restoring antitrust enforcement against mergers and dominant-firm conduct after decades of narrowing court doctrine—is aimed squarely at concentrated market power that the bill's own findings link to higher prices, lower wages, and harder market entry. The tradeoffs are real: stricter standards and heavy penalties risk chilling some legitimate deals and conduct, and much depends on how regulators and courts apply the new rules. But the design includes safeguards, such as a preponderance-of-evidence defense for merging parties and procompetitive-benefit defenses for exclusionary conduct.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on February 4, 2021, with Senators Blumenthal, Booker, Markey, and Schatz as original cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary on February 4, 2021; the bill received no further action of any kind.
Nine Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican did, and the bill never advanced past committee referral before the 117th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Dominant corporations in concentrated markets—especially large technology platforms and habitual acquirers—avoided stricter merger review, an exclusionary-conduct ban, and penalties of up to 15% of US revenue. The two federal antitrust agencies also kept operating under existing budgets.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Dominant corporations that avoided stricter antitrust rules

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its push in the Senate.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it stayed at the referral stage for the rest of the Congress.

against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed and lobbied against expanding antitrust enforcement during the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill advanced no further than committee referral.

industries.industry: Large technology platforms and other dominant firms
industries.note: The bill creates a presumption that exclusionary conduct by firms with over 50% market share is unlawful, imposes penalties up to 15% of total US revenue, and lowers the bar for blocking their acquisitions. These firms' gains from market power come at the direct expense of consumers, competitors, and workers.

industries.industry: Corporate acquirers and merger-active industries (private equity, telecom, hospitals, agribusiness)
industries.note: Mergers over $5 billion, or by firms over $100 billion acquiring anything over $50 million, would have to prove they don't harm competition—a reversal of the current setup where the government must prove harm. Sectors that have consolidated heavily through serial acquisitions would face the largest constraint.

industries.industry: Federal antitrust agencies (DOJ Antitrust Division, FTC)
industries.note: The bill authorizes $484.5 million for the Antitrust Division and $651 million for the FTC, roughly triple their prior budgets, and creates a new Office of the Competition Advocate within the FTC. Their interest in expanded authority and funding runs alongside better enforcement on behalf of consumers.

The bill only directs the FTC to study whether common ownership of rivals by institutional investors harms competition; it imposes no new rules on them yet. But the study could be a step toward regulation of common ownership.

industries.industry: Antitrust defense bar and corporate legal departments
industries.note: Stricter standards, shifted burdens of proof, and heavy penalties would generate substantially more antitrust litigation, increasing legal spending by companies while increasing demand for antitrust counsel on both sides.
